text: Metformin, available under the brand name Glucophage among others, is the primary first-line medication for treating type 2 diabetes, especially in individuals who are overweight. It is also used in the management of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and is sometimes used off-label to reduce the risk of metabolic syndrome in patients on antipsychotic medications. Metformin inhibits inflammation and does not cause weight gain; it is taken orally. It is generally well tolerated, with common adverse effects including diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain, and has a low risk of causing low blood sugar. A rare but serious concern is high blood lactic acid levels (lactic acidosis), which can occur with excessive dosing or in individuals with severe kidney disease. Metformin is a biguanide anti-hyperglycemic agent that works by reducing liver glucose production, increasing insulin sensitivity in body tissues, and stimulating GDF15 secretion, which reduces appetite and caloric intake. First described in 1922 by Emil Werner and James Bell, it was studied in humans by French physician Jean Sterne in the 1950s and introduced as a medication in France in 1957. It is included on the World Health Organization’s List of Essential Medicines and is available as a generic. In 2023, it was the second most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with over 85 million prescriptions, and ranked among the top 10 most prescribed medications in Australia between 2017 and 2023. The American Diabetes Association and American College of Physicians recommend metformin as first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes, and it is as effective as repaglinide and more effective than other oral drugs for this condition. Evidence suggests metformin is associated with weight loss in obesity without diabetes, and it has a lower risk of hypoglycemia than sulfonylureas, though hypoglycemia can occur during intense exercise, calorie deficit, or when combined with other glucose-lowering agents. Metformin modestly reduces low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride levels. A 2019 systematic review found moderate-quality evidence that metformin reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in prediabetes compared to diet and exercise or placebo, but no significant benefit when compared to intensive diet or exercise, and no advantage when added to such interventions. In women with PCOS, tentative evidence shows metformin increases live birth rates, especially in those who have not responded to clomiphene, though it does not appear to affect miscarriage risk. An updated Cochrane review found no conclusive evidence of improved live birth rates when metformin is used before or during IVF/ICSI, with uncertainty in long GnRH-agonist protocols and possible increases in clinical pregnancy rates, while short GnRH-antagonist protocols may reduce live birth rates. Metformin may reduce the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but could increase side effects. Evidence does not support general use during pregnancy to improve maternal or infant outcomes in obese women. The UK’s National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence recommended metformin for women with PCOS and a BMI over 25 for anovulation and infertility when other treatments fail, though international guidelines do not recommend it as first-line or at all, except for those with glucose intolerance, and instead favor clomiphene and lifestyle changes. Metformin reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in women with PCOS who have impaired glucose tolerance at baseline. In Poland, metformin is approved and reimbursed for PCOS. A review comparing metformin to insulin in gestational diabetes found good short-term safety for mother and baby, but long-term safety remains unclear. Several studies found metformin as effective and safe as insulin for gestational diabetes, with women gaining less weight and having a lower risk of pre-eclampsia, and babies having less visceral fat, which may reduce later insulin resistance. However, babies born to mothers treated with metformin have lower birth weights initially but show accelerated postnatal growth and are heavier by mid-childhood, a pattern linked to long-term cardiometabolic disease. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis found metformin to be safe and effective in managing diabetes in pregnancy with no adverse effects on mother or child after eleven years of follow-up. Metformin is typically associated with weight loss and is effective in counteracting weight gain from antipsychotics like olanzapine and clozapine, though primary prevention is more beneficial. In type 1 diabetes, metformin may reduce insulin requirements but increases hypoglycemia risk. Metformin is contraindicated in people with severe kidney disease, though it may be used at lower doses in those with mild to moderate kidney disease, with dose adjustments based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and periodic kidney function monitoring. The FDA advises avoiding metformin when eGFR falls below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m². Lactic acidosis is rare during routine use, with incidence rates around nine per 100,000 persons per year, similar to background rates, and no definitive evidence links metformin to lactic acidosis. The risk increases with massive overdose, though large doses are often not fatal. Cimetidine and cephalexin can increase metformin plasma concentrations by competing for renal tubular secretion. Anticholinergic medications may increase metformin absorption by slowing gastric motility, raising plasma levels and adverse effect risk. The exact molecular mechanism of metformin is not fully understood, but proposed mechanisms include inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), inhibition of glucagon-induced cAMP production, inhibition of mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and effects on gut microbiota. Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production, decreases growth hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone secretion, and improves insulin sensitivity in liver, muscle, endothelium, adipose tissue, and ovaries. The average person with type 2 diabetes has three times the normal rate of gluconeogenesis, which is reduced by over one-third with metformin. AMPK activation is required for metformin’s inhibition of liver glucose production and for increased expression of small heterodimer partner, which suppresses hepatic gluconeogenic genes. Metformin increases cytosolic AMP, which may allosterically activate AMPK, or bind to PEN-2, though the exact mechanism remains uncertain. It inhibits cyclic AMP production, blocking glucagon action and lowering fasting glucose. Metformin also alters the gut microbiome, increasing agmatine production, which may contribute to its effects. Due to its effects on GLUT4 and AMPK, metformin is described as an exercise mimetic. It has an oral bioavailability of 50–60% under fasting conditions and is absorbed slowly.

Metformin exhibits insulin-independent glucose uptake and some of its metabolic effects occur via AMPK-independent mechanisms, though AMPK likely has a modest overall effect and is not directly responsible for decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis.[120][121] In women with insulin resistance, such as those with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), metformin has indirect antiandrogenic effects due to improved insulin sensitivity, potentially reducing testosterone levels by up to 50%, although a Cochrane review found only slight effectiveness in lowering androgen levels in PCOS.[122][123] Metformin also influences the gut microbiome by increasing agmatine production by gut bacteria, though the relative importance of this mechanism compared to others remains uncertain.[124][125][126] Due to its effects on GLUT4 and AMPK, metformin is described as an exercise mimetic.[127][128] It has an oral bioavailability of 50–60% under fasting conditions and is absorbed slowly; peak plasma concentrations (Cmax) occur within 1–3 hours for immediate-release formulations and 4–8 hours for extended-release forms.[8][129] Metformin has negligible plasma protein binding and a high apparent volume of distribution (300–1000 L after a single dose), with steady state typically reached in 1–2 days.[8] Its acid dissociation constants (pKa) are 2.8 and 11.5, meaning it exists predominantly as a hydrophilic cationic species at physiological pH, with less than 0.01% nonionized in blood; the nonionized form has low lipid solubility (logP = −1.43), indicating poor passive diffusion through cell membranes and a reliance on the SLC22A1 transporter for cellular entry.[130][131] The logP of metformin is lower than that of phenformin (−0.84) because two methyl groups on metformin confer less lipophilicity than phenformin’s larger phenylethyl side chain; more lipophilic derivatives are being studied as prodrugs to improve oral absorption.[132] Metformin is not metabolized and is excreted unchanged in urine via tubular secretion, with undetectable levels in blood plasma within 24 hours of a single dose; its average plasma elimination half-life is 6.2 hours, though red blood cell concentrations show a longer half-life of 17.6 hours (ranging from 18.5 to 31.5 hours in nondiabetic single-dose studies), suggesting accumulation in red blood cells.[8][133] Some evidence indicates that liver metformin concentrations may be two to three times higher than plasma levels due to portal vein absorption and first-pass uptake after oral administration.[121] Metformin hydrochloride (1,1-dimethylbiguanide hydrochloride) is freely soluble in water, slightly soluble in ethanol, and almost insoluble in acetone, ether, or chloroform; its pKa is 12.4.[134] The original synthesis of metformin in 1922 involved a one-pot reaction of dimethylamine hydrochloride and 2-cyanoguanidine under heat; according to the 1975 Aron patent and the Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Encyclopedia, equimolar amounts of dimethylamine and 2-cyanoguanidine are dissolved in toluene with cooling, followed by slow addition of equimolar hydrogen chloride, resulting in self-boiling and precipitation of metformin hydrochloride with 96% yield; excess HCl forms the more soluble metformin dichloride salt, a recently reported impurity.[137][138][139] In December 2019, the U.S. FDA learned that some metformin products manufactured outside the U.S. contained low levels of N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), a probable human carcinogen; Health Canada and the European Medicines Agency also assessed NDMA levels.[140][141][142] In February 2020, the FDA found NDMA levels in tested samples did not exceed acceptable daily intake; Health Canada recalled Apotex immediate-release metformin, followed by recalls of Ranbaxy and Jamp metformin in March; in May 2020, the FDA asked five companies—Amneal Pharmaceuticals, Actavis Pharma, Apotex Corp, Lupin Pharma, and Marksans Pharma Limited—to voluntarily recall sustained-release metformin products; in June 2020, the FDA published lab results showing NDMA in certain extended-release metformin lots and recommended recalls of lots exceeding the 96 nanogram per day acceptable intake limit, and it began sharing testing results with international regulators; in July 2020, Lupin Pharmaceuticals recalled all lots of metformin after detecting unacceptably high NDMA levels; in August 2020, Bayshore Pharmaceuticals recalled two lots of tablets; in September 2024, the FDA issued revised guidelines on nitrosamine impurities.[158] The biguanide class, including phenformin and buformin, originates from the plant Galega officinalis (Goat's rue), which has been used in folk medicine for centuries; however, G. officinalis does not contain biguanides, which are chemically synthesized compounds composed of two guanidine units and designed to be less toxic than the plant-derived guanidine and galegine.[159] Metformin was first described in 1922 by Emil Werner and James Bell as a product in the synthesis of N,N-dimethylguanidine; in 1929, Slotta and Tschesche discovered its sugar-lowering effect in rabbits, identifying it as the most potent biguanide analog studied, though this finding was overlooked as other guanidine analogs and insulin gained prominence.[160][161] Interest in metformin resumed in the late 1940s when it was found not to affect blood pressure or heart rate in animals; in 1950, Filipino physician Eusebio Y. Garcia used metformin (named Fluamine) to treat influenza, noting it lowered blood sugar to minimum physiological levels without toxicity and believed it had bacteriostatic, antiviral, antimalarial, antipyretic, and analgesic effects; in 1954, Polish pharmacologist Janusz Supniewski failed to confirm most of these effects, including blood sugar reduction, and observed antiviral effects in humans.[163][164][165][166][167] French diabetologist Jean Sterne, prompted by Garcia’s report, reinvestigated metformin and other biguanide analogs at Laboratoires Aron in Paris; he was the first to administer metformin to humans for diabetes treatment, coined the name "Glucophage" (glucose eater), and published results in 1957.[161][168] Metformin was introduced in France in 1957 and entered the British National Formulary in 1958, being sold in the UK by Rona.[15][169] Broad interest revived in the 1970s following the withdrawal of other biguanides; metformin received approval in Canada in 1972 and in the U.S. by the FDA for type 2 diabetes in 1994; Glucophage, produced under license by Bristol-Myers Squibb, was first marketed in the U.S. on March 3, 1995; generic formulations are available in several countries.[170][171][168] The U.S. FDA granted orphan drug designation for metformin, and the European Medicines Agency granted orphan drug status.[172][173][174] Metformin and its major metabolite guanylurea are found in wastewater treatment plant effluents and regularly detected in surface waters, with concentrations above 200 μg/L measured in the German river Erpe, among the highest reported for pharmaceutical transformation products.[175] Metformin is the British Approved Name (BAN), United States Adopted Name (USAN), and International Nonproprietary Name (INN); common brand names include Glucophage, Riomet, Fortamet, and Glumetza in the U.S., and Obimet, Gluformin, Dianben, Diabex, Diaformin, Metsol, Siofor, Metfogamma, and Glifor elsewhere; all but liquid formulations have generic equivalents.[176][177][178] Metformin is often prescribed in combination with other medications, with fixed-dose combinations available to reduce pill burden, cost, and simplify administration.[179][180] A metformin/rosiglitazone combination (Avandamet) was released in 2002 and sold by GlaxoSmithKline or as a generic, with formulations of 500/1, 500/2, 500/4, 1000/2, and 1000/4 mg; it was the most popular metformin combination in 2009; in 2005, Avandamet was removed from the market due to violations of good manufacturing practices, though it was reintroduced by the end of that year and a generic version from Teva received FDA tentative approval and reached the market in early 2012; following a 2007 meta-analysis linking rosiglitazone to increased heart attack risk, concerns arose, leading the European Medicines Agency to recommend suspension in 2010, and subsequent withdrawals in the UK, India, New Zealand, and South Africa; from November 2011 to November 2013, the FDA restricted rosiglitazone and metformin/rosiglitazone sales to prescription-only, requiring risk notifications and mail-order purchases; in November 2013, the FDA lifted these restrictions after the 2009 RECORD trial showed no elevated risk of heart attack or death.[190][191][192][193][194][195][196][197] Metformin/pioglitazone combinations (Actoplus Met, Piomet, Politor, Glubrava) are available in the U.S. and European Union.[198][199][200][201][202] Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors reduce glucagon and blood glucose levels; DPP-4 inhibitor combinations with metformin include sitagliptin/metformin (Janumet), saxagliptin/metformin (Kombiglyze XR, Komboglyze), and alogliptin/metformin (Kazano, Vipdomet); linagliptin/metformin is sold as Jentadueto and is available as a generic in the U.S. as of August 2021.[203][204][205][206][207][208][209][210][211][212] Metformin is also combined with SGLT2 inhibitors dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and canagliflozin; sulfonylureas increase insulin release from pancreatic beta cells; a 2019 systematic review found limited evidence on whether metformin combined with sulfonylurea improves mortality or complications compared to other glucose-lowering therapies, and such combinations were associated with a higher risk of hypoglycemia; metformin is combined with glipizide (Metaglip) and glibenclamide (glyburide, Glucovance), with generic formulations available (glibenclamide more popular); meglitinides (nateglinide and repaglinide) bind to beta cells similarly to sulfonylureas but with different receptor affinities and shorter durations, requiring higher blood glucose levels to initiate insulin secretion; repaglinide/metformin is sold as Prandimet or its generic; combinations of metformin with dapagliflozin and saxagliptin are available in the U.S. as Qternmet XR; metformin with pioglitazone and glibenclamide is available in India as Accuglim-MP, Adglim MP, Alnamet-GP, and in the Philippines as Tri-Senza; metformin with pioglitazone and lipoic acid is available in Turkey as Pional; metformin is a pleiotropic drug with extensive off-target activity beyond its antidiabetic effects, largely attributed to AMPK activation, though other mechanisms are proposed; it is under investigation as a potential agent to delay aging and may increase longevity in animal models such as C. elegans and crickets.[221][222][234][235][236][131]

The combination of metformin with dapagliflozin and saxagliptin is available in the United States as Qternmet XR. The combination of metformin with pioglitazone and glibenclamide is available in India as Accuglim-MP, Adglim MP, and Alnamet-GP; and in the Philippines as Tri-Senza. The combination of metformin with pioglitazone and lipoic acid is available in Turkey as Pional. Metformin is a pleiotropic drug with extensive off-target activity beyond its antidiabetic effects, much of which is attributed to its action on AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), although other mechanisms have been proposed. Metformin is under investigation for its potential to delay aging; it may increase longevity in some animal models, such as C. elegans and crickets, and this effect may be mediated by insulin and carbohydrate regulation, similar to its effects on diabetes. Whether metformin may help extend life in otherwise healthy people remains unknown; a 2021 review found it is likely to improve healthspan rather than lifespan. A 2017 review found that people with diabetes taking metformin had lower all-cause mortality and reduced cancer and cardiovascular disease compared with those on other therapies; however, in people without diabetes, metformin does not appear to reduce the risk of cancer or cardiovascular disease. The potential anti-cancer effects of metformin are believed to be mediated through AMPK activation and IGF-1R modulation, with research focusing particularly on stomach cancer, showing evidence of protective impact and improved survival rates in patients with developed cancer, though evidence remains preliminary and there is no consensus on its preventive or therapeutic role. A study found a benefit using metformin to reduce the occurrence of long COVID. It is unclear if metformin reduces the risk of death in people with COVID-19. There has been extensive research into the potential neuroprotective effects of metformin in developmental and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, other dementias, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, certain types of epilepsy, and fragile X syndrome, with mixed results. Preliminary studies have examined whether metformin can reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease and whether there is a correlation between type 2 diabetes and the risk of Alzheimer's disease. While metformin may reduce body weight in persons with fragile X syndrome, whether it improves neurological or psychiatric symptoms is uncertain. A derivative HL156A, also known as IM156, is a potential new drug for medical use.
